text:
Predicates:
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
Employee(x) ::: x is an employee.
Schedule(x) ::: x schedules a meeting with their customers.
LunchAtHome(x) ::: x has lunch at home.
LunchAtCompany(x) ::: x has lunch in the company building.
WorkRemotely(x) ::: x works remotely from home.
InOtherCountry(x) ::: x is in other countries.
Premises:
∀x (Employee(x) ∧ Schedule(x) → Appear(x)) ::: All employees who schedule a meeting with their customers will go to the company building today.
∀x (LunchAtCompany(x) → Schedule(x)) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company building schedules meetings with their customers.
∀x (Employee(x) → LunchAtHome(x) ⊕ LunchAtCompany(x)) ::: Employees have lunch either in the company building or at home.
∀x (LunchAtHome(x) → WorkRemotely(x)) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, they are working remotely from home.
∀x (InOtherCountry(x) → WorkRemotely(x)) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
∀x (Manager(x) → ¬WorkRemotely(x)) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
Manager(james) ↔ Appear(james) ::: James will appear in the company today if and only if he is a manager.
Conclusion:
(Manager(james) ∨ InOtherCountry(james)) → ¬(LunchAtHome(james) ∨ WorkRemotely(james)) ::: If James is either a manager or in other countries, then James does not either have lunch at home or work remotely from home.
(LunchAtHome(james) ∨ WorkRemotely(james)) → ¬(Manager(james) ∨ InOtherCountry(james)) ::: If James either has lunch at home or works remotely from home, then he is neither a manager nor does he work in other countries.
